item.title: Best-of-N Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description:
Best-of-N Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models

Researchers have identified a critical flaw in best-of-N test-time steering methods for vision-language-action (VLA) models, where increasing the number of candidates can lead to reward hacking when the verifier is inaccurate. The study demonstrates that higher values of N cause selected candidate rewards to diverge from accurate verifier rewards, favoring candidates that exploit prediction errors rather than true performance gains. This effect was systematically examined across 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a π₀.₅ policy with ten repetitions per case, revealing that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can provide partial mitigation against this phenomenon.

item.title: DexEngine Converts Human Hand Motions into Robot-Executable Data at Scale
item.description:
DexEngine Converts Human Hand Motions into Robot-Executable Data at Scale

📚 Introduction

A new pipeline called DexEngine has been introduced to convert human hand-object demonstrations into large-scale, physically executable trajectories for training robotic manipulation policies.

🧩 How It Works

DexEngine processes human motion data in three stages:

  • Places each clip’s hand-object motion where robot arms can reach it
  • Finds an arm motion that follows the human hands
  • Corrects the motion in physics simulation using residual reinforcement learning

⚙️ Key Details

The system generates substantial amounts of training data:

Metric Value
Datasets Processed 9 human hand-object datasets
Clips per Hand 5,200
Total Trajectories 65,000 (116 h)
Total Episodes 325,000 (578 h)

Key findings include:

  • Policies trained on data corrected by DexEngine outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with arms attached after a floating-hand correction
  • Fine-tuning on physics-corrected data is essential for performance
  • Mid-training on the generated data provides additional improvements in both simulation and on real robots
  • DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods
  • The pipeline operates more than 10x faster than reinforcement learning-based alternatives

💡 Why It Matters

The research demonstrates that depth coverage is more critical than measurement precision for learned manipulation policies. Additionally, the findings highlight that policies trained on clean depth data lose performance when holes appear during deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These insights suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should be evaluated based on depth coverage rather than measurement precision.

🚀 Availability

The work is classified under Computer Science > Robotics and was submitted on 25 Nov 2026. The paper is available for viewing in PDF and HTML formats.

#Robotics #ImitationLearning #DexEngine #Manipulation #DepthSensing

Source: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT Source: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data

item.title: Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation
item.description:
Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation

A new research paper titled “Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation” has been submitted to arXiv under Computer Science and Robotics on November 25, 2026.

🔍 Overview

When a lead robot cannot continue a route, researchers investigate what it should send to the teammate that must finish the route. The study explores this by replaying a frozen receiver at each contact under alternative messages in vision-and-language navigation.

⚙️ Key details

  • Across 3,920 autonomous departures in 106 environments, adding the view before the lead’s last action block to its executed actions raised success by 7.51 percentage points (pp) per RxR handoff and 8.54 pp per SAGE handoff.
  • Per departure, the gains were 2.23 pp and 1.44 pp, respectively.
  • At contact, the lead had accumulated a median of 41 frames.
  • Sending one frame when available recovered 24% of the full-history advantage over actions alone in SAGE and 30% in RxR.
  • Over an estimated progress cue in SAGE, the image rescued 100 routes and reversed 54 successes.
  • Near-goal receivers finished outside less often, dropping from 63.1% to 51.7% post hoc.
  • Earlier views outperformed the contact view by 6-7 pp per handoff in secondary comparisons.
  • Gains were detectable from about 7 kB per handoff.
  • Random transmission matched within size bins nearly equaled the learned sender’s team success.
  • The lead continuing in simulation defines the empirical full-history ceiling (Solo).
  • Exact-route specificity and image gains at controlled starts with mostly unknown progress or outside the goal region remained unresolved.

#Robotics #ComputerVision #AI #Navigation

Source: Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation

item.title: New AI Development Framework TRIAGE Optimizes Model Selection and Adaptation
item.description:
New AI Development Framework TRIAGE Optimizes Model Selection and Adaptation

Researchers have introduced TRIAGE, a novel framework for selecting and adapting public AI checkpoints to specific deployment scenarios. The approach addresses how organizations can effectively utilize pre-trained models without training from scratch by systematically identifying and repairing gaps between model capabilities and deployment requirements.

🧩 How it Works

TRIAGE operationalizes the selection and adaptation process through a structured five-stage pipeline:

  • Sensors and latency requirements are evaluated first with non-overridable gates
  • Local data is probed across ten minutes of operational logs
  • Model ranking occurs based on target-relevant performance among candidates passing initial gates
  • Fine-tuning proceeds with closed-loop monitoring before release
  • All stages maintain feasibility checks throughout the adaptation process

⚙️ Key Details

The framework distinguishes three distinct gap types that determine adaptation strategy:

Gap Type Repairability Description
Sensing gap Cannot be closed with sensor data Information sensors fail to capture
Latency gap Belongs to control loop, not weights Output arrives after control needs it
Distribution gap Fine-tuning can repair Mismatches between training and deployment data

Critical findings from implementation include:

  • Driving benchmarks demonstrate that latency below leading model thresholds causes 80-90% collision rates
  • Field of view loss causes 2.2-5.7x more planning errors than equivalent resolution loss
  • Local frames reduce stability gaps by 75% but increase perturbation sensitivity at limited budgets
  • Score-based selection violated gates in 2 of 4 deployment profiles tested

🚀 Availability

Real-world testing validated TRIAGE’s effectiveness:

  • Factory camera initially failed sensing gate; additional camera resolved the issue
  • Latency gate eliminated two highest-scoring candidates that couldn’t complete closed-loop trips
  • Selected model achieved acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trials
  • Closed-loop validation rejected a fine-tuned model that showed offline improvement

💡 Why It Matters

TRIAGE enables organizations unable to train foundation models from scratch to:

  • Determine whether public checkpoints are compatible with their specific hardware
  • Identify necessary modifications when compatibility issues arise
  • Implement monitored adaptation processes that balance performance with safety constraints

#AI #machinelearning #modeloptimization #robotics #computervision

Source: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform

item.title: New AI Method CondUQ Enables Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification
item.description:
New AI Method CondUQ Enables Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification

Researchers have introduced CondUQ, a novel approach for conditional uncertainty quantification in machine learning systems that improves safety-critical applications requiring accurate error estimation. The method addresses shortcomings of existing techniques that cannot accurately model how errors vary with input quality and operating conditions.

📊 Overview

The CondUQ framework was submitted on 25 Nov 2026 and focuses on reliability- and safety-critical applications that need precise uncertainty quantification for measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. Unlike single Gaussian models or unconditional approaches, CondUQ conditions error models on observable factors to enable more accurate uncertainty quantification.

🧩 How it works

CondUQ operates through two key stages:

  • Maps observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors with the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution
  • Trains the QI predictor end-to-end using a distribution-matching objective without requiring quality labels
  • Fits and calibrates a Gaussian error model for each QI on a large held-out dataset

The approach is designed to integrate with existing systems without modification and works even with black-box systems.

⚙️ Key details

The CondUQ method was demonstrated across three diverse examples:

Application Error Type Conditioning Factors
GPS system Multipath errors Satellite elevation and signal strength
Visual system Relative attitude errors Internal features of image pairs
World model Prediction errors Input observations and actions

In all cases, CondUQ substantially reduced discrepancies between modeled and empirical error distributions compared to single global models. The learned quality indices also revealed how underlying factors affect error characteristics in ways consistent with physical principles.

🚀 Availability

The research is available as an arXiv preprint with options to view PDF or HTML formats. Associated code and data resources include connections to platforms like Hugging Face, DagsHub, and other development frameworks.

#uncertainty #machinelearning #CalibratedUQ #safety #reliability

Source: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching

item.title: New DFLAT Algorithm Enables Subsecond Long-Horizon Kinodynamic Planning for Tractor-Trailers
item.description:
New DFLAT Algorithm Enables Subsecond Long-Horizon Kinodynamic Planning for Tractor-Trailers

Researchers have introduced DFLAT, a diffusion-based planning algorithm that achieves subsecond planning times for long-horizon kinodynamic trajectory optimization, particularly enabling practical deployment of tractor-trailer maneuvering systems. DFLAT addresses the long-standing trade-off between scalability and feasibility in diffusion-based motion planning for kinodynamically constrained systems by operating directly on differentially flat trajectory representations.

🧩 How it works

DFLAT denoises a compact set of Hermite curve parameters in the flat-output space, consisting of intermediate waypoints together with endpoint tangents of each segment. Rather than diffusing over time-discretized controls, it operates in a more efficient parameter space where every denoised sample maps to a dynamically consistent trajectory.

🔍 Overview

The algorithm produces feasible trajectories by construction rather than requiring restoration after generation, eliminating the need for post-processing steps that typically slow down planning. This approach enables DFLAT to match or exceed the success rates of existing baselines while maintaining consistently lower planning times across various benchmark scenarios.

⚙️ Key details

Experiments demonstrate that where traditional kinodynamic RRT requires over 100 seconds, DFLAT plans in subsecond time. The method particularly excels on long-horizon problems requiring multiple forward-reverse maneuvers, making it especially valuable for complex tractor-trailer operations that involve intricate spatial reasoning.

🚀 Availability

The research was submitted on 25 November 2026 and includes associated code, data, and media resources through the arXiv platform’s ecosystem, including alphaXiv, DagsHub, Hugging Face, and other research infrastructure tools.

#robotics #motionplanning #diffusionmodels #kinodynamics #trajectoryoptimization

Source: DFLAT: Model-based Diffusion on Differentially Flat Spaces for Long-Horizon Trajectory Optimization

item.title: New LSRP*-LA Planner Solves Large-Agent MAPF with Scalable Asynchronous Coordination
item.description:
New LSRP*-LA Planner Solves Large-Agent MAPF with Scalable Asynchronous Coordination

Researchers have introduced LSRP*-LA, a novel multi-agent path finding (MAPF) planner designed for large agents with asynchronous actions. Unlike prior approaches, LSRP*-LA scales to 800 agents, improves solution quality over time, and delivers near-optimal results for complex scenarios involving agents that occupy multiple cells.

📌 Overview

Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) aims to calculate collision-free paths for multiple agents moving from start to goal locations while minimizing total path costs. Traditional MAPF methods assume:

  • Each agent occupies a single vertex
  • All agents act synchronously

These constraints limit real-world applicability. Existing planners that relax both assumptions either struggle with scalability or fail to refine solutions effectively.

🧩 What’s New

The newly proposed LSRP*-LA addresses these limitations by supporting:

  • Large agents that occupy multiple cells
  • Asynchronous actions among agents

It builds upon LSRP*, a prior scalable and anytime planner with asynchronous capabilities, extending it to handle spatially larger agents.

⚙️ Key Details

Feature Description
Scalability Handles up to 800 agents on diverse maps
Anytime Improvement Continues enhancing solution quality post-initial output
Path Cost Efficiency Achieves roughly half the cost of synchronous planners for large agents
Agent Size Support Designed specifically for agents occupying multiple cells

🚀 Availability

The paper titled “LSRP-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions”* was submitted on 25 Nov 2026. A PDF and experimental HTML version are available online.

💡 Why It Matters

LSRP*-LA represents a significant advancement in robotics planning by overcoming two major limitations in existing MAPF algorithms. Its ability to scale efficiently while improving paths over time makes it especially valuable for deployments involving numerous spatially complex agents.

#multi-agentpathfinding #roboticsplanning #asynchronousagents #pathfindingalgorithm #scalableAI

Source: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions

item.title: New MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld Environment Helps Diagnose AI Reasoning Failures
item.description:
New MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld Environment Helps Diagnose AI Reasoning Failures

Researchers have introduced MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld, an interactive maze environment designed to attribute specific causes of failure in vision-language models during reasoning tasks. The environment isolates distinct mechanisms to help identify why models fail, including misreading the environment, not understanding component operations, incorrect action ordering, and failure to recover from mistakes.

🧩 How it works

MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld allows researchers to add, modify, or remove four types of mechanisms independently while keeping the renderer, action space, and scoring function unchanged:

  • Key-door pairs
  • Switch-gate pairs
  • Distractors and decoys
  • Ordered combinations of these mechanisms

A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state provides every maze instance with an exact optimal action count, which determines difficulty and grades incomplete episodes.

⚙️ Key details

The evaluation protocol was fixed on 15 held-out mazes across 540 episodes, then used to test three vision-language models on 50 mazes. Results showed:

  • Only 6 of 150 episodes were solved
  • 45 of 50 mazes remained unsolved by any model
  • No episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was successfully solved

🚀 Availability

The work was submitted on 2 September 2026 by Pranav Guruprasad and is available on arXiv under the Computer Science > Machine Learning category. Experimental HTML and PDF versions are accessible through the arXiv platform.

#AI #MachineLearning #VisionLanguageModels #Benchmarking #MultiNet

Source: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments Source: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills

item.title: RoboARC benchmarks robot manipulation under precise spatial constraints
item.description:
RoboARC benchmarks robot manipulation under precise spatial constraints

RoboARC is a new benchmark designed to test whether robot agents can reason out the correct motions for hard manipulation tasks that hinge on exact spatial constraints. The collection features 90 tasks across six constraint types, involving both rigid and soft materials, evaluated in MuJoCo simulation on three different robot platforms.

🧩 How it works

Each task is structured as a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Tasks are provided in two evaluation regimes:

  • Privileged regime: Full simulator state access and resets allowed
  • Standard regime: Real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) with a single attempt and no resets

Seven coding agents and four vision-language-action (VLA) policies—none trained on these tasks—were evaluated against the benchmark.

⚙️ Key details

The strongest performer was GPT-6 Astra in Codex, which achieved:

  • 86% success rate in the Privileged regime
  • 43% success rate in the Standard regime

The four VLA policies, evaluated zero-shot, solved none of their 18 one-arm puzzles.

Analysis of 15 tasks that GPT-6 Astra solved in Privileged but failed in Standard revealed that:

  • Object poses alone added 4 points (from 24% to 28%)
  • Part geometry alone added 13 points (from 24% to 37%)
  • Both object poses and part geometry together added 36 points (from 24% to 60%)

Only 7% of the coding agents’ failed runs passed more than half of a task, and 53% of failed runs in the Standard regime were stuck on a single step. The results show that frontier coding agents can reason out correct motions once they know object locations and shapes, but performance drops significantly when relying solely on sensor inputs in a single attempt.

🚀 Availability

The RoboARC benchmark is available at the project website.

💡 Why it matters

The findings highlight that spatial constraint understanding remains a critical gap in robotic manipulation. While agents can reason about motion when given complete scene information, real-world sensor limitations significantly reduce performance. The benchmark provides a standardized evaluation framework for future research in constraint-based manipulation tasks.

#robotics #manipulation #benchmark #spatial #AI

item.title: Ada-BFM Adapts Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction
item.description:
Ada-BFM Adapts Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction

Ada-BFM, a post-training framework, adapts behavior foundation models for humanoid scene interaction while preserving pretrained whole-body control capabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • BFMs emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose humanoid control through pretraining on large-scale behavioral data.
  • Their proficiency in whole-body coordination does not readily extend to scene interaction, which requires adapting motion to scene-dependent geometric constraints and contact dynamics.
  • Ada-BFM is introduced as a post-training framework that adapts pretrained BFMs for humanoid scene interaction.

🧩 How it works

  • Ada-BFM augments the original architecture with a lightweight adapter, enabling interaction-specific adjustments while leveraging pretrained control capabilities.
  • Rather than producing a separate controller for each task, the framework yields a shared model for each interaction domain.
  • This shared model supports diverse tasks involving terrain or object interaction.

⚙️ Key details

  • Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that Ada-BFM enables diverse scene interaction behaviors.
  • Ada-BFM accelerates learning compared with training from scratch.
  • Ada-BFM largely preserves pretrained behavioral competence.

💡 Why it matters

  • These findings establish Ada-BFM as an effective and efficient approach to extending the capabilities of BFMs beyond their pretraining settings.
  • The approach retains the strengths of BFMs in general whole-body control.
  • Title: Ada-BFM: Adapting Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction
  • Submitted on 24 Nov 2026

item.title: MARGIN Agent Reduces Robot Program Execution Risk via Near-Miss Evidence
item.description:
MARGIN Agent Reduces Robot Program Execution Risk via Near-Miss Evidence

Robot-programming agents typically improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, but binary success metrics often saturate while execution risk remains high in unseen scenes. MARGIN is a new risk-aware agent designed to address this by converting successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement.

🧩 How it works

MARGIN introduces a signal called the near-miss margin, which measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this metric to:

  • Prioritize fragile programs.
  • Guide targeted repairs.
  • Select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom.

Additionally, the system employs an exact safe-racing rule to accelerate the evaluation of success-based candidates.)

⚙️ Key details

The performance and reliability of MARGIN have been evaluated across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. Key findings from the evidence include:

Metric / Observation Result
LIBERO-Pro Development Success In an 80-task reproduction, 78 programs attained perfect development success despite substantial failures on unseen seeds
Risk Prediction The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774
Failure Risk Low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk
Execution Efficiency MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0% across two independent evaluation rounds on 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks
Cross-Benchmark Efficiency Executed control step reductions of 18.0-20.0% observed on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite
Evaluation Efficiency Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections

Paired execution probes further improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions during the refinement process.

💡 Why it matters

These results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement, addressing the gap where standard binary success metrics fail to capture execution risk in unseen environments.

#Robotics #AIAgents #ControlPolicies #RiskAwareness #LIBERO

Source: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement

item.title: New Benchmark CALVIN-MAX Tests Robot Policies Under Dynamic World Changes
item.description:
New Benchmark CALVIN-MAX Tests Robot Policies Under Dynamic World Changes

📚 Introduction

Robots must often keep working after the world changes, for example when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. A new benchmark, CALVIN-MAX, introduces 7,828 test cases to measure how robot policies handle such changes during task execution.

🧪 Key Details

  • CALVIN-MAX contains 7,828 cases built on CALVIN’s five-instruction chains.
  • Each case includes one change to either the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction.
  • The benchmark compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins.

The three runs serve distinct purposes:

Run Type Description
Run 1 (without change) Reference scenario with no modification
Run 2 (change from that moment) The changed world starts when the instruction begins
Run 3 (change during motion) The change arrives while the robot is already moving
  • Comparing Run 2 to Run 1 measures the cost of the changed world.
  • Comparing Run 3 to Run 2 measures the effect of handling the change mid-motion.

📊 Performance Impact

On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over eight core changes.

Timing matters for certain change types:

  • Changes that alter what the robot sees reduce success by 5.4 points less when introduced mid-motion compared to starting with the change in place.
  • Changes to the scene itself or to the robot show no detectable difference between timing conditions.

⏱️ Long-Term Effects

  • Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the mid-motion benefit for every policy.
  • In a stricter test, the rewound run must match Run 2 to pass—this succeeds for three policies.
  • The cost of a change can persist beyond the affected instruction: if the change remains in place, a policy that completes the first instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

🚀 Availability

  • CALVIN-MAX is publicly available as a benchmark for evaluating robot policies under dynamic conditions.

#robotics #benchmarking #AI-evaluation #CALVIN #robot-policies

Source: CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?

item.title: New BendGS Method Enables Joint-Angle-Free Self-Modeling for Continuum Robots
item.description:
New BendGS Method Enables Joint-Angle-Free Self-Modeling for Continuum Robots

Intro

A new AI development called BendGS enables continuum robots to predict their next 3D shape, appearance, and tip pose from observed images without relying on measured joint angles or fixed link geometry, addressing a key limitation in existing visual self-modeling approaches.

🔍 Overview

  • Visual self-models learn from images how a robot moves under motor commands.
  • Continuum robots need them even more, as they bend continuously without measured joint angles or fixed link geometry.
  • Existing continuum self-models predict point clouds, image-space curves, or future images, but not the next 3D shape, appearance, and tip pose together from an observed body.
  • 3D Gaussians offer a renderable representation of shape and appearance, yet articulated Gaussian self-models rely on joint angles to drive deformation.

🧩 How it works

  • BendGS uses a virtual backbone estimated from observation to drive command-conditioned Gaussian deformation, enabling next-state prediction for continuum robots without measured joint angles.
  • In Gaussian modeling, a feed-forward network reconstructs the robot as 3D Gaussians from multi-view images, and the backbone, a chain of coordinate frames, is fitted to back-projected depth points to estimate the bending state.
  • In transition, a network predicts its change under a relative motor command to deform the bound Gaussians.
  • The deformed Gaussians render the next images and the 3D shape, and the distal frame gives the tip pose.

⚙️ Key details

  • Training losses use RGB-D images and masks, without bending or tip labels.
  • On simulated and real robots, BendGS achieves the lowest Chamfer distance, best image quality, and lowest tip errors among the compared methods.

🚀 Availability

  • BendGS: Observation-Conditioned Gaussian Self-Modeling for Continuum Robots
  • [Submitted on 24 Nov 2026]
  • Computer Science > Robotics

item.title: New Deployment Method Bridges Real Vehicle Gap for Autonomous Driving Models
item.description:
New Deployment Method Bridges Real Vehicle Gap for Autonomous Driving Models

Intro

A new deployment methodology called Released-to-Real (R2R) addresses the gap between high-performing autonomous-driving models and their real-world vehicle deployment. The approach corrects source-system coupling while improving success rates and sensor accuracy.

🔍 Overview

The research identifies why released autonomous-driving models struggle when deployed on new real vehicles. Even after conventional adaptation, these models remain coupled to assumptions from their source sensing, data, and execution processes.

🧩 How it works

R2R Methodology

  • Identifies source-system coupling in released models
  • Corrects only affected components while preserving the original model
  • Achieves sensor adaptation across multiple released detectors and three real sensor rigs

Human-Anchored Reinforcement Learning (HA-RL)

  • Corrects trajectory-level optimization mismatch through recorded target driving data
  • Avoids costly rollouts of generative closed-loop reinforcement learning
  • Operates on the ego state rather than observation inputs

Sensor Adaptation

  • Localizes and corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations
  • Uses frozen perception weights
  • Requires neither target annotations nor retraining

⚙️ Key Details

Component Description
HA-RL Corrects ego state mismatch for data and behavior adaptation
Sensor Adaptation Handles physical sensor adaptation with frozen weights
Multi-Camera Support Improves multi-camera detector performance on target rigs

item.title: New robotics research addresses VLA brittleness with neuro-symbolic integration
item.description:
New robotics research addresses VLA brittleness with neuro-symbolic integration

Several new robotics papers submitted on 23 Nov 2026 address persistent barriers in real-world robot deployment, focusing on reliability, safety auditing, and robustness under coupled uncertainties.

🧩 Proposed Frameworks

Researchers have introduced multiple methodologies to overcome the limitations of current end-to-end systems, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which often exhibit brittle generalization and inconsistent motor control under distribution shifts.

  • Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: A deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning, and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints.
  • Collision Rendering: The first trajectory planning framework on sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR), supporting GPU-accelerated, risk-bounded collision checking and differentiable collision cost.
  • Co-DRIS + SuperMimic: A perception-action co-design framework for reactive robotic manipulation that couples an inertial world-frame physics-informed world model with an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder.
  • RESET: A framework that reconstructs contact-rich worlds from a single real demonstration to enable self-improvement of robot manipulation skills without runtime LLM calls.

  • Collision Rendering: Approximates robots with collision spheres and uses a probabilistic collision model to derive upper bounds on directional collision probability via a GPU-accelerated rendering pipeline. It integrates with sampling-based planners without auxiliary geometric maps.
  • Co-DRIS + SuperMimic: Addresses the degradation seen in single-frame frameworks (like DRIS) when perception and actuation uncertainties co-occur. It includes phase-aware variable-impedance soft-catching that transitions a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm into an overdamped regime.
  • RESET: Uses open-loop replay and silhouette consistency to examine reconstructed worlds, evolving modular white-box task graphs from per-node failure evidence. It allows skills to be shared with unseen robots without new demonstrations.

Current VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit safety constraints, making assurance difficult in safety-critical settings. item.title: POISE: Curvature-Aware Critic Regularization for Smooth Actor-Critic Control
item.description:
POISE: Curvature-Aware Critic Regularization for Smooth Actor-Critic Control

🎯 Overview

PAV inger-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature.

🧩 How it works

The same gradient change, however, moves the critic’s preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further shows that the shift’s curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged.

⚙️ Key details

  • On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by 5.9× on average (4.5× geometric mean), compared with 2.2× (1.9×) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks.
  • Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

item.title: RoboTrack: New Benchmark, Dataset, and Models for Point Tracking in Robotics
item.description:
RoboTrack: New Benchmark, Dataset, and Models for Point Tracking in Robotics

Today we release RoboTrack, a new benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation, along with two new models.

🔍 Overview

  • RoboTrack‑Bench contains 307 human‑annotated videos from DROID, Ego‑Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse. 2,522 point tracks are annotated and verified by humans.
  • Videos capture robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first‑ and third‑person viewpoints.
  • Annotators prioritize points that move or become occluded, use TAP‑Vid motion estimates to trace each point, and label each track as belonging to a robot/human body, a manipulated object, or a static object.
  • A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame.
  • RoboTrack‑Bench includes 33 video pairs recorded simultaneously from two cameras, with the same physical points annotated in both views.

🧩 How it works

  • The pipeline extends MolmoSpaces, Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories.
  • This produces RoboTrack‑15M, a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.
  • Two new point tracking models are released:
    • RoboTracker: a fine‑tuned AllTracker model using RoboTrack data and techniques.
    • RoboTracker‑Warp: trained from CoWTracker.

⚙️ Key details

  • Evaluations show that leading trackers score 3.0 to 6.6 AJ lower on RoboTrack‑Bench than on the only other real‑video robotics benchmark, RoboTAP.
  • The strongest off‑the‑shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 AJ on RoboTrack‑Bench.
  • Adding RoboTrack‑15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks.
  • RoboTracker improves average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines.
  • RoboTracker‑Warp achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on four of the five benchmarks evaluated.

🚀 Availability

  • We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet‑lab tasks.
  • Both RoboTrack components and the two new models are publicly released.

💡 Why it matters

  • RoboTrack‑Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks, exposing weaknesses across multiple tracker architectures and training data.
  • Synthetic data from RoboTrack‑15M can boost real‑world performance and cross‑benchmark generalization.

item.title: LangForce updates VLA-Arena results and accepts to ICML 2026
item.description:
LangForce updates VLA-Arena results and accepts to ICML 2026

LangForce has released updated performance metrics on the VLA-Arena benchmark and received acceptance to ICML 2026. The framework addresses a specific pathology in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model training known as Information Collapse, where models degenerate into vision-only policies by ignoring language constraints.

🧩 How it works

LangForce tackles the Vision Shortcut problem by forcing models to ground actions in language rather than relying solely on visual observations. It employs a dual-branch architecture and Bayesian decomposition to optimize policies.

  • Bayesian Decomposition: The model explicitly estimates a vision-only prior $p(a \mid v)$ and a language-conditioned posterior $\pi(a \mid v, \ell)$.
  • Latent Action Queries: Learnable queries are used to decouple vision-only and language-conditioned action distributions.
  • Optimization Objective: The policy maximizes the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between actions and instructions, effectively penalizing vision shortcuts and rewarding language-grounded actions.

📊 Updated Performance

The team has updated LangForce results on VLA-Arena, achieving average success rates of:

Benchmark Level Success Rate
L0 84.2%
L1 38.8%
L2 24.1%

Additional experiments on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa demonstrated an 11.3% improvement on the out-of-distribution (OOD) SimplerEnv benchmark using the exact same datasets as baselines. This approach also helps prevent the catastrophic forgetting of general multimodal reasoning capabilities common in standard VLA fine-tuning.

item.title: Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion
item.description:
Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion

Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. This approach is particularly effective in tasks with multiple phases, where the budget must be divided among them.

🔍 Overview

  • Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion by correcting an imitation-trained base policy.
  • The method is applied to tasks with several phases, requiring the budget of environment interaction to be divided among these phases.

🧩 How it works

  • The completion gain is formalized as the change in full-task completion probability when a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy’s action during a single phase.
  • The completion gain is decomposed into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase.
  • Positive estimates of the completion gain determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases.

⚙️ Key details

  • In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, but the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase.
  • Gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget.
  • In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release.
  • In a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

item.title: New Method Improves Vision-Language Models for Dexterous Robot Hands
item.description:
New Method Improves Vision-Language Models for Dexterous Robot Hands

🔍 Overview

Researchers have developed a method to enhance Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for dexterous robotic manipulation, addressing a key limitation: most datasets use parallel-jaw grippers, making transfer to multi-fingered hands difficult. This work explores fine-tuning strategies to adapt VLAs for dexterous hands using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL).

🧩 How it works

The study evaluates five fine-tuning approaches with a LEAP hand and two simulation tasks, using only a few demonstrations. Key techniques include:

  • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) paired with Diffusion-Steering Reinforcement Learning (DSRL) to adapt VLAs for dexterous manipulation.
  • Freezing the Vision-Language Model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert for better steerability.
  • Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) as a less effective approach compared to other methods.

The research identifies three critical insights:

  • SFT success does not correlate well with post-DSRL effectiveness, meaning optimal SFT checkpoints are not always the best for steering.
  • Freezing the VLM and training the action expert alone yields the most effective policy.
  • LoRA is the least steerable fine-tuning approach.

⚙️ Key details

Fine-Tuning Recipes Evaluated

Recipe Description Key Insight
Freezing VLM, tuning action expert Most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements
SFT with DSRL Insight 1: SFT success ≠ post-DSRL success
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) Least steerable approach

Evaluation Metrics

  • Tasks: Two simulation tasks using a LEAP hand.
  • Demonstrations: Only a handful of demonstrations used.
  • Success Rate: 86.7% success in 30 trials across two cylinder sizes in simulation.
  • Tactile Framework: Introduced TacPilot—a tactile residual framework for selective updates around a frozen visual policy.

🚀 Availability

  • Code/Data: Associated with the paper on platforms like Hugging Face, DagsHub, and alphaXiv.
  • TacPilot Framework: Validated on OpenArm v2 with Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich tasks.

💡 Why it matters

This research provides a practical framework for improving the adaptability of VLAs to dexterous robotic hands, reducing reliance on extensive teleoperation datasets. By focusing on action expert tuning and avoiding SFT rollout success as a checkpoint metric, the method enhances the robustness and efficiency of robotic manipulation systems.

item.title: New Robotic Manipulation Methods: RePlan-VLA, LAGR, and GTI
item.description:
New Robotic Manipulation Methods: RePlan-VLA, LAGR, and GTI

Three new approaches address distinct challenges in robotic manipulation: managing long-horizon task execution, selecting task-oriented grasps, and maintaining semantic intent over multiple stages. These methods aim to improve reliability and success rates in complex physical environments by refining how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and grasping detectors process state and context.

📋 RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning

A new framework called RePlan-VLA addresses performance degradation in VLA models on long-horizon tasks involving multiple interdependent manipulations.

  • Core Logic: It leverages the VLA’s existing short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework, rather than burdening the policy with long-horizon reasoning, memory, or error recovery.
  • Mechanism: The framework explicitly monitors robot motion for progress evaluation and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes.
  • Compatibility: It is VLA-agnostic and preserves the underlying policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning.
  • Performance:
    • Achieves a 21.9% improvement in success rate over the next strongest baseline on the RoboCasa365 benchmark.
    • Achieves a 10.4% improvement on the CALVIN benchmark.
    • Validated for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

🤏 LAGR: Task-Oriented Grasp Detection

The LAGR method and its accompanying dataset address the need for grasps that are both physically feasible and suitable for specific downstream tasks (e.g., holding a hammer by the handle for use vs. the head for handover).

  • Dataset: A newly constructed dataset contains 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations across 100,911 image-task pairs from 17 object categories.
  • Architecture:
    1. Generates task-independent grasp proposals with a physical feasibility score.
    2. Uses a language-conditioned re-ranker to score these proposals jointly.
  • Results:
    • Outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points.
    • Validated on real objects using a Franka Research 3 robot.

🎯 GTI: Grounding Task Intent

GTI (Grounding Task Intent) ensures that global task intent remains grounded in the currently executable context during long-horizon manipulation.

  • How it Works: Uses current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase.
  • Visual Targets: For each local subtask, it generates two phase-dependent visual targets:
    • An interaction/contact state.
    • A local completion state.
    • These targets, alongside the local language instruction, jointly condition the VLA to specify both current actions and target states.
  • Recovery: Includes anomaly monitoring and local recovery mechanisms (rollback, re-observation, phase re-evaluation) to re-establish intent consistency after persistent deviation.
  • Performance Gains:
    • RoboCasa365: GR00T success on seen composite tasks increases from 14.6% to 31.8% (Identity Distribution) and from 12.1% to 20.4% (Out-of-Distribution) compared to matched Global-FT baselines.
    • VLA-Arena: GTI + $\pi_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with significant gains on harder L1/L2 tasks.
    • Real-World: Mean full-task success on PiPER tasks increases from 21.7% to 59.2%.

item.title: PIBT*_T Enables Fast Turn‑Aware Path Planning for Hundreds of Mobile Robots
item.description:
PIBT*_T Enables Fast Turn‑Aware Path Planning for Hundreds of Mobile Robots

A new algorithm, PIBT*_T, accelerates multi‑agent path planning by handling turn actions explicitly.

🔍 Overview

  • Large‑scale multi‑mobile‑robot systems require fast and reliable path planning under realistic motion constraints.
  • MAPF_T explicitly models orientation changes and turn‑induced delays, but these constraints increase the computational burden of search‑based methods.
  • Priority‑inheritance‑based planning offers a highly scalable alternative, yet directly extending it to MAPF_T is nontrivial because turn actions break the immediate node‑vacation assumption underlying conventional priority inheritance.

🧩 How it Works

  • PIBT*_T is an efficient iterative solver for MAPF_T.
  • It preserves the lightweight single‑timestep planning mechanism of Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT) while introducing dedicated mechanisms to handle:
    • Turn‑induced dependencies
    • Local deadlocks
    • Livelock
    • Inefficient repeated pushing

⚙️ Key Details

  • Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks show that PIBT*_T achieves high success rates and strong scalability, solving instances with up to 1000 agents within seconds.
  • For realistic engineering environments, Action Dependency Graph (ADG)-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study demonstrate that turn‑aware planning better reflects robot execution and reduces actual makespan compared with classical MAPF planning.
  • Experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical feasibility of the proposed method.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Enables scalable coordination of hundreds of robots by explicitly modeling turns.
  • Improves real‑world execution efficiency through accurate turn‑aware planning.
  • Shows that priority‑inheritance techniques can be extended to complex action models without sacrificing scalability.

item.title: Radar Doppler Measurement Improves Safety Control for Dynamic Obstacles
item.description:
Radar Doppler Measurement Improves Safety Control for Dynamic Obstacles

Researchers present a radar-native control barrier function that uses FMCW radar Doppler measurements directly as the derivative of a range-based barrier function, reducing estimation delay in safe robot control around dynamic obstacles.

🔍 Overview

  • Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires both distance and relative motion information.
  • Traditional range-based filters reconstruct range rate from successive range measurements or obstacle-state estimators, introducing estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes.
  • FMCW radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler.
  • This work uses the Doppler measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF), yielding a closed-form filter on the robot’s forward velocity.

🧩 How It Works

  • Direct Doppler measurement replaces the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop.
  • A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing.
  • The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections.

⚙️ Key Details

  • In 508 paired encounters within the platform’s retreat capability:
    • Direct Doppler: 2 buffer incursions
    • Constant-acceleration Kalman filter: 15 buffer incursions
    • Constant-velocity Kalman filter: 25 buffer incursions
  • On a Unitree Go1 quadruped, the controller stops at 0.777 ± 0.015 m (predicted 0.758 m) and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.
  • This approach improves safety performance in dynamic environments with fewer buffer incursions compared to estimator-based methods.

#Radar #ControlBarrierFunctions #Robotics #Safety #FMCW #Doppler

Source: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative

RadixQuantVLA, an active‑development framework, unifies post‑training quantization, benchmarking, and deployment preparation for Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models.

RadixQuantVLA follows a modular, pipeline‑oriented view. Each route is a composable block that includes a model loader, quantization method, calibration context, benchmark suite, output artifact, and validation record. Calibration data, sensitivity analysis, layer protection, and route‑specific artifacts are treated as first‑class engineering objects.

  • Uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn diverse behaviors
  • Robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs
  • Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery
  • Temporary assistance facilitates exploration during training

item.title: RoboDx Benchmark Evaluates AI Repair of Robot Navigation Software
item.description:
RoboDx Benchmark Evaluates AI Repair of Robot Navigation Software

Researchers have introduced RoboDx, a benchmark for evaluating how well AI models can diagnose and repair faults in simulated robot navigation software. The benchmark reveals that passing unit tests does not guarantee correct robot behavior, and that even verified repairs often fail to address all injected faults — especially undocumented configuration constants.

🔍 Overview

  • RoboDx generates repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults
  • Includes 100 tasks in the RoboDx-Hard-100 set
  • Features a hidden verifier that only marks repairs verified if the robot drives correctly in hidden scenarios the agent never sees
  • Contains two evaluation tracks: one with code visible, another where code is hidden and the agent must pick the cause from a list of hypotheses

🧩 How It Works

  • Hidden verification: A repair is marked verified only if the robot drives correctly in hidden scenarios not shown to the agent
  • Two-fault tasks with quiet faults: A quiet fault makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present
  • Diagnostic track: Models receive measurements from the faulty robot, selected so only the true cause produces all of them in the simulator
  • Hypothesis selection: When code is hidden, agents choose from a list of hypothesized causes

⚙️ Key Details

Aspect Detail
Total tasks analyzed 94
Single-fault tasks 44
Two-fault tasks 50
Verified repairs by Claude Opus 5.5 (two-fault tasks) 49 of 50
Verified repairs removing both injected edits 17 of 49
Opus naming both faults without seeing code 10 of 50
Models naming true cause from measurements (max) 38 of 94
Models with simulator output for every hypothesis Right on almost all
Gain from models’ own predictions of simulator output No detectable gain
Real bug-fix PR tasks evaluated 97
  • Most faults left behind after verified repairs are configuration constants whose correct values the task documentation does not state
  • On real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5 scored lowest among four models tested; the other three models showed no clear ordering

💡 Why It Matters

  • Unit tests alone are insufficient for validating robot navigation repairs
  • Verification via hidden driving scenarios catches patches that pass unit tests but drive the robot off course
  • Even when repairs pass verification, they frequently fail to fix all faults — particularly undocumented configuration values
  • Diagnostic ability from raw measurements remains limited across current models
  • Access to simulator outputs for hypotheses dramatically improves diagnostic accuracy, but models’ own predictions provide no benefit

item.title: Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities
item.description:
Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities

Recent research introduces two distinct frameworks addressing key challenges in zero-shot robot navigation: RPSI-Nav for recursive policy self-improvement in multi-object search, and ROMUX for navigation using uncalibrated exocentric cameras.

🧩 How RPSI-Nav Works

RPSI-Nav forms a recursive loop where the system revises both its navigation program and the revision mechanism itself:

  • Diagnoses search behavior and requests diagnostic views when observations cannot distinguish competing causes
  • Generates targeted navigation revisions based on diagnosis
  • Links feedback from subsequent goal searches to the rules that produced revisions
  • Updates the improver (diagnosis, observation acquisition, revision planning) to govern future improvements
  • Conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals

🧩 How ROMUX Works

ROMUX predicts metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images without camera calibration:

  • Trains a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict obstacle maps from exocentric images
  • Does not condition image tokens on camera information (pose or intrinsics)
  • Uses a small PPO-trained policy to navigate on predicted maps toward goal coordinates relative to the robot
  • Works with single or multiple cameras with partial views
  • Transfers zero-shot to real robots with cameras at varying positions and orientations across room layouts

⚙️ Key Details

Framework Task Key Innovation
RPSI-Nav Zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation Recursive self-improvement of both policy and improvement mechanism
ROMUX Point-goal navigation with obstacle avoidance Cross-view transformer predicting metric maps from uncalibrated, unknown exocentric cameras

💡 Why It Matters

  • RPSI-Nav addresses the constraint where fixed human-designed revision mechanisms limit continued self-improvement in navigation policies
  • ROMUX eliminates time-consuming calibration requiring specialized personnel, which must be repeated when cameras move or new rooms are navigated
  • Both systems operate zero-shot in unseen environments without training or fine-tuning
  • Benchmark experiments and real-robot evaluations validate both approaches
  • ROMUX matches success rates of policies using robot-mounted cameras in simulation with randomized cameras per episode

🚀 Availability

  • RPSI-Nav: Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations completed
  • ROMUX: Benchmarked in simulation with per-episode camera randomization; transferred zero-shot to real robot across various room layouts and camera positions/orientations

item.title: XMimic Trains Humanoid Motion Tracking 3.7x Faster Than BlinkMimic
item.description:
XMimic Trains Humanoid Motion Tracking 3.7x Faster Than BlinkMimic

🚀 Overview

XMimic is a new AI development that trains whole-body motion tracking for the Unitree G1 robot 3.7 times faster than the previous BlinkMimic method when using four H100 GPUs. The improvement comes from rebuilding BlinkMimic’s world-model trainer in JAX, enabling faster training while maintaining the same quality.

🧩 How it works

XMimic implements the same algorithm as BlinkMimic but runs entirely in JAX. This includes the simulator (MuJoCo Warp through MJX), the replay buffer, the world model, the policy and the critic. The entire training iterations compile into single XLA programs, so the GPU never waits for Python. The system can distribute iterations across 2 to 4 GPUs working simultaneously.

⚙️ Key details

  • Speed: Reaches BlinkMimic’s target in 0.86 minutes on four H100s (vs. 3.19 minutes on one); on a single H100, XMimic is 1.3 times faster
  • Quality: Both methods achieve the same normalized evaluation return (0.86–0.87) with no clip failures after 6 minutes of training
  • Target: Normalized evaluation return ≥ 0.82 with none of the 40 LAFAN1 clips failing, held for three consecutive checkpoints
  • GPU usage: Uses slightly more total GPU time (3.4 vs. 3.2 GPU-minutes) but the speedup buys wall-clock time
  • Hardware: One H100 NVL per GPU, GPUs connected by NVLink in a node
  • Training: All methods ran on the same cluster; every 100th checkpoint is evaluated on all 40 clips with 4 replicas each
  • Hyperparameters: Uses BlinkMimic’s hyperparameters (PRESET[main], commit d264658)

The development is detailed in the paper XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute by Nico Bohlinger and Jan Peters (2026).

📄 Availability

XMimic replaces the first version which covered XMimic alone. It is accompanied by XSoma, which applies the same recipe for locomotion on rough terrain. Please cite the paper if you use XMimic:

item.title: NVIDIA Introduces Open Source SOMA Retargeter for Humanoid Motion Adaptation
item.description:
NVIDIA Introduces Open Source SOMA Retargeter for Humanoid Motion Adaptation

The open source NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter adapts human motion data to fit a humanoid robot’s specific proportions, joint structures, and ranges of motion. Built around the shared human-motion representation in NVIDIA SOMA-X, the tool provides capabilities to configure robot embodiments, refine motion, and process trajectory data for downstream learning or control systems.

⚙️ How It Works

Directly copying human joint movement is not feasible for humanoid robots due to differences in physical structure. SOMA Retargeter adapts motion through a standardized workflow:

  • Input: Reads a Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) animation represented on the SOMA base skeleton.
  • Processing: Scales motion targets to the robot’s proportions, solves configured inverse-kinematics objectives for joint poses per frame, and applies configured post-processing corrections.
  • Output: Generates a comma-separated values (CSV) file containing the robot’s root position, orientation, and joint angles for each frame.

🧩 Compatible Motion Sources

Human motion inputs can be unified on the SOMA skeleton representation across multiple capture and generation methods:

Source / Tool Function Description
BONES-SEED Motion Capture Collection of human motion-capture data.
GEM-X Video Reconstruction Reconstructs whole-body 3D human motion from a single video using the SOMA body model.
Kimodo Motion Generation Generates human motion sequences from text and pose constraints on the SOMA skeleton.
ARDY Motion Generation Generates movement from text and pose constraints with interactive steering as motion unfolds.

🚀 SOMA Retargeter v0.2 Release

The v0.2 release includes sample motions from the BONES-SEED dataset, reference retargeting results, and pre-built configurations for five humanoid robot embodiments:

  • Unitree G1
  • Unitree H2
  • Booster T1
  • AgiBot X2 Ultra
  • AgiBot A3T3

To retarget a sample forward walk using the Unitree G1 configuration, users open a terminal in the repository root and start the viewer:

uv run python app/bvh_to_csv_converter.py --config assets/default_bvh_to_csv_converter_config.json --viewer gl

With unitree_g1 selected by default, selecting Retarget on the BVH Motion row under Scene Options → Motion executes the scaling, inverse-kinematics solving, and post-processing. The viewer displays the resulting robot animation alongside the source human motion.

item.title: NVIDIA Holoscan 5 Adds Integrated Robotic Control and Streamlined Sensor Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA Holoscan 5 Adds Integrated Robotic Control and Streamlined Sensor Processing

NVIDIA announced Holoscan SDK version 5, introducing built‑in robotic control alongside its existing low‑latency sensor‑processing capabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • Holoscan 5 combines low‑latency control with high‑throughput perception in a single programming model.
  • The SDK supports both CPU‑centric motor‑control loops and heavy‑throughput GPU algorithms, including AI inference.
  • A new, lightweight programming model makes it easy to integrate Holoscan into existing code bases and to move data in and out of Holoscan graphs.

🧩 How it works

  • Operators & Graphs – The core concepts remain Operators and Graphs.
  • Partitions – Chains of operators are grouped on a single thread, avoiding cross‑thread handoffs and unnecessary syscalls, which reduces latency and jitter.
  • Timing contracts – Operators express when work should run using clock and data‑arrival triggers; bounded, drop‑oldest queues prevent stale work from building up.
  • Compiled plan – Before the first run, the plan reveals the execution strategy and catches configuration errors.
  • NVTX annotations – Built‑in annotations expose operator execution and message transfers in Nsight Systems, and the SDK also provides Nsight Systems annotations for latency and jitter inspection.

⚙️ Key details

  • Robotic control is now a first‑class feature, demonstrated on the Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601‑DM, which uses quasi‑direct‑drive actuators for high torque bandwidth.
  • The tutorial uses Pinocchio as the inverse‑dynamics solver (URDF model + Recursive Newton–Euler Algorithm) and the motorbridge library for joint feedback and motor commands.
  • Both libraries implement the same three‑operator control loop.
  • Supports 10 kHz CPU‑centric motor‑control loops while maintaining stable torque‑oriented performance.
  • Tested on:
    Platform OS
    Jetson Orin Nano Ubuntu 24.04
    Jetson Thor Ubuntu 24.04
    x86 Ubuntu 24.04
  • Requires Python 3.12 or newer on Linux.
  • Configuration includes checking the serial device and motor IDs in the arm’s configuration file.
  • The tutorial repository’s technical guide covers configuration, math, and hardware startup.

🚀 Availability

  • The walkthrough can be run on a real robot, with the SDK’s Nsight Systems annotations used to inspect latency and jitter.
  • All supported platforms (Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson Thor, x86 Ubuntu 24.04) are ready for deployment.

💡 Why it matters

  • Torque‑oriented projects such as haptic devices and collaborative robots need rapid, consistent feedback at hundreds or thousands of hertz; any runtime overhead or thread handoff can introduce phase lag and destabilize the system.
  • By eliminating cross‑thread handoffs, providing deterministic timing contracts, and exposing execution plans early, Holoscan 5 gives developers a clear path to stable, high‑performance robotic control on edge hardware.

item.title: FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning
item.description:
FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning

Today a new framework called FoundationWorlds was introduced, pairing a controlled simulated world with tools for automatically generating tasks, training demonstrations, and metrics to measure a robot’s behavior over time.

🔍 Overview

  • The first FoundationWorld is ToyBlocks, an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop.
  • ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations – recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation – without requiring time‑consuming teleoperation.
  • It builds on earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces.

🧩 How it works

  • Skill generation uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning in Isaac Lab, Nvidia’s open‑source framework for robot learning in simulation.
  • Policies learn non‑prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up.
  • Skill generation can draw on privileged information (exact block position and orientation) that a real robot cannot sense, enabling automatic creation of skills that would otherwise need teleoperation.
  • A task‑and‑motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences skills to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them.
  • Each plan run in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations with labels describing the performed task or skill.
  • Data generation scales by running hundreds of plans in parallel on a single GPU, achieving up to 24 × real‑time performance.

⚙️ Key features

  • Designed around four requirements:
    1. Realistic physics and appearance
    2. Automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale
    3. Challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity
    4. Broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain
  • Blocks display pictures and letters, enabling searching, sorting, and arranging tasks.
  • A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs.
  • Domain randomization varies block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene to test generalization.
  • High‑level reasoning models decide what to do; low‑level action models control the robot’s movements.
  • Molmo 2 selects skills (e.g., rotation, flipping) via a pointing interface; ManiFlow executes the commanded skills on the simulated arm.
  • The controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets.

💡 Why it matters

  • ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain, providing realistic physics, automatic data generation, and a blend of reasoning and dexterity challenges.
  • By training models from raw sensor observations, the framework bridges the gap between simulation and real‑world perception problems.

item.title: Goal-Branching LaCAM Improves Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
item.description:
Goal-Branching LaCAM Improves Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding

Goal-Branching LaCAM introduces temporary goals to help a multi‑agent pathfinding solver handle dense, corridor‑heavy environments.

🔍 Overview

  • LaCAM is a search‑based solver for Multi‑Agent Pathfinding (MAPF) that performs a depth‑first search over joint configurations.
  • It uses PIBT (Priority Inheritance with Backtracking) to generate successors and lazily adds single‑agent constraints to explore alternatives.
  • While complete, LaCAM struggles on dense maps because deadlocks often require coordinated moves of several agents away from their goals, which PIBT’s greedy one‑step successors rarely propose.

🧩 How Goal‑Branching Works

  • The paper proposes Goal‑Branching, where blocking agents receive temporary goals.
  • Each temporary goal is explored as an additional branch of LaCAM’s search.
  • Random and corridor‑aware rules are examined for selecting these temporary goals.
  • Completeness is preserved for any such rule.

⚙️ Key Results

Metric Goal‑Branching LaCAM LaCAM*
Solve rate on dense instances (60‑90% occupancy) 89% 44%
First‑solution speedup on maze‑32‑32‑2 and room‑32‑32‑4 (instances both solve) 10‑14× faster Baseline
Median time speedup at 75% density on room‑32‑32‑4 ~200× faster Baseline
Solution cost increase on instances both solve 15‑22% higher Baseline
Solution cost on open maps and full MovingAI benchmark No higher than LaCAM* (≤3% slower) Baseline

💡 Why It Matters

  • By adding temporary goals, the solver can break deadlocks without enumerating constraints agent by agent.
  • The approach retains the completeness of the original algorithm while dramatically improving success rates and runtime on challenging dense maps.
  • Cost overhead is modest and disappears on less congested environments.

Submitted on 5 Nov 2026

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA has added four open‑weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family, enabling interactive world simulation and multi‑sensor, multi‑view driving scene generation.

🔍 Overview

  • The new checkpoints are built on the Cosmos 3 Nano architecture and each contains 16 B trainable parameters.
  • All models are released under OpenMDW 1.1, which permits both commercial and non‑commercial use.
  • They target
    • offline synthetic driving data creation,
    • fast streaming simulation,
    • text‑guided visual rendering, and
    • bimanual robot interaction.

🧩 How it works

  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto generates synchronized video from up to 11 camera views (including fisheyes) and joint RGB‑LiDAR data. It uses per‑camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls for scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto is a causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer‑Auto. It produces small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in a few denoising steps, leveraging generated history and updated driving controls for long, interactive rollouts. A simulation runtime and WSM renderer are required to update controls from driving inputs.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer takes simulator controls and a text prompt to render photorealistic video observations. The physics and ground‑truth state remain with the simulator; the text prompt only influences appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual predicts video based on robot or camera actions. It supports two‑arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controllable by a policy or human‑operated joysticks. Training used 59 control values padded to 64, with a schema that defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains.

⚙️ Key details

  • Open weight: All four checkpoints are open‑weight and can be post‑trained on user data to match specific camera layouts, LiDAR configurations, or environments.
  • Multi‑sensor sync: Camera and LiDAR streams are generated together, linking visual observations with 3‑D sensing.
  • Control flexibility: Scene and traffic‑signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, enabling study of driving‑policy responses.
  • Streaming interaction: Streaming generation ties video prediction to ongoing interaction, allowing exploration of how actions and observations unfold together.
  • Licensing: Released under OpenMDW 1.1, allowing commercial and non‑commercial use.

🚀 Availability

The four checkpoints—Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer, and Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual—are now available as open‑weight models in the Cosmos 3 family.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides researchers with open tools for generating realistic driving data across many sensors and viewpoints.
  • Enables fast, interactive simulation of driving scenarios, supporting closed‑loop policy evaluation.
  • Extends simulation capabilities to robotic manipulation with bimanual actions, broadening the scope of world‑model research.

item.title: Tau Robotics Deploys Remotely Piloted Humanoid Cleaning Robots in San Francisco
item.description:
Tau Robotics Deploys Remotely Piloted Humanoid Cleaning Robots in San Francisco

I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

🤖 Overview

  • Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes.
  • The robots are piloted remotely by humans who watch what’s happening via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists.
  • While cleaning, the robots collect data that Tau will use to train more independent descendants.

🛠️ How it works

  • Human pilots perform motions on a control interface; sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them (kinematic guidance).
  • Tasks that need kinematic guidance include making the bed and folding laundry; these produce especially valuable training data.
  • The robots communicate with Tau’s headquarters through a 3D‑printed “head” with antennae.
  • A short signal transmission delay can affect coordination, causing the robot to walk “strangely.”
  • Overheating of the remote‑operator’s equipment can cause the robot to stall.

⚙️ Robot specifications

  • Height: four‑and‑a‑half‑foot‑tall.
  • 3D‑printed head with antennae for communication.
  • Two 3D‑printed claw “hands” (human‑like hands were found not durable enough).
  • Grippy socks to avoid scratching hardwood floors.
  • Each robot wears a Tau Robotics shirt.

📋 Capabilities

  • Can vacuum and mop without any human help.
  • With kinematic guidance, can make the bed and fold laundry.
  • In a later visit, cleaned a kitchen, tackled a toilet, and re‑attached a cleaning wand three times by poking it into place.
  • Struggles with stairs, often climbing with a “drunk” gait and occasional backward stumbles.

💰 Pricing

  • $30 for an hour‑long cleaning with a single robot (initial offering).
  • $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots (current rate).
  • $100 for a one‑time visit (current rate).
  • Even at $30 per hour, the robots are thorough but slow, making self‑cleaning potentially more efficient.

🚧 Limitations & Incidents

  • Stair navigation is unreliable; the robot can stagger backward.
  • Overheating can cause the robot to stall; in one case the remote‑operator’s equipment shut down.
  • Without remote assistance, the robot cannot clean.
  • The robot is slow, and watching it for the entire visit may not be an efficient use of time.

🚀 Future outlook

  • Tau’s long‑term goal is to make fully autonomous cleaning robots a reality.
  • Data collected during current remotely‑piloted cleanings will be used to develop more independent descendants.

item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot

NVIDIA demonstrated an end‑to‑end workflow that uses RTX Spark, Isaac Lab, and Omniverse tools to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy for the Microduck robot, and evaluate the policy in Isaac Sim.

🔍 Overview

  • Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires perception, balance, and the ability to adjust actions when obstacles block the path ahead, not just a walking policy.
  • The development process links three stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model robot‑environment interaction, and training + evaluating policies in simulation.

🛠️ Tools and Roles

Component Role
RTX Spark Local development hub; supports AI‑assisted planning, policy validation, and receives trained policies for local evaluation in Isaac Sim.
Isaac Lab Cloud‑based robot‑learning framework for reinforcement learning.
Newton Models physical behavior for simulation.
Omniverse libraries Generate simulated visual observations via RTX rendering.
Isaac Sim Runs local evaluation of trained policies returned from RTX Spark.
Hermes Translates prompts into step‑by‑step project plans and creates asset inventories from images.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Works with Hermes to generate project plans and analyze images for reusable assets.
Astra Builds and tests assets; directs FreeCAD geometry creation and Blender material application.
SimReady Central Library Free, ungated library of >2,000 simulation‑ready OpenUSD assets.
Microduck Reference quadruped robot used for navigation training.

📐 Workflow Steps

  1. Write a natural‑language prompt that describes the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn.
  2. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate the prompt into a detailed project plan (task, resources, outputs, stages).
  3. Review official Microduck documentation and summarize its capabilities, constraints, and unknowns.
  4. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
  5. Generate a photorealistic concept image using a verified Microduck reference image.
  6. Hermes and Nemotron analyze the concept image, extract unique reusable assets, assign identifiers, and create cropped reference images.
  7. Astra enhances the references, models geometry in FreeCAD, and adds fine details and materials in Blender.
  8. Assemble the assets into a simulated environment; Newton provides physics, Omniverse renders visuals.
  9. Train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab in the cloud using the simulated environment.
  10. Return the trained policy to RTX Spark and evaluate it locally in Isaac Sim.
  11. Verify robot capabilities, test navigation, obstacle handling, and reset logic—all in simulation (no physical hardware).
  12. Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions for reproducibility.

📊 What You’ll Learn

  • How to create a simulated obstacle course for a quadruped robot.
  • How AI agents (Hermes, Nemotron, Astra) automate planning, asset extraction, and 3D modeling.
  • How to train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab and validate it with RTX Spark and Isaac Sim.
  • How to leverage the SimReady Central Library for reusable simulation assets.
